opus-5.5.text:
So, historically, AGI was meant to be a system capable of performing in any domain a human could perform in. That was the original idea: generality across domains, as opposed to narrow systems that play chess or recognize faces. And the reason we needed a separate term was that, early on, AI researchers were promising general intelligence and kept delivering narrow tools, so the "general" had to be made explicit.

Superintelligence is a step beyond that. It's a system that is superior to all humans in all domains: better at science, better at engineering, better at persuasion, better at strategy, better at AI research itself. And that last part is crucial, because once a system is better than us at designing the next system, you get this self-improvement dynamic, and the gap between human-level and superhuman may not be very long at all.

Now, if you look at current systems, I think if you took one of today's large models back twenty years and showed it to an AI researcher, many would say, "Yes, this is AGI." It writes code, it writes poetry, it passes professional exams, it translates, it does math at a fairly high level. It's not perfect; it makes mistakes, it hallucinates, it struggles with long-horizon planning. But humans make mistakes too. So in a lot of ways we already have weak forms of general capability, and we keep moving the goalposts because each time something is achieved we say, "well, that's not real intelligence."

I also think the comparison to "human level" is a bit misleading. We're not one level. There's huge variation between people, and there are many domains where these systems are already superhuman in breadth: no human knows that many languages and that many fields at once. In other domains they're still behind. So it's not a single line we cross; it's a jagged frontier, and different capabilities cross it at different times.

What concerns me is that regardless of what we call it, the trend is clear. Capabilities keep growing with more compute and more data, and our ability to control, explain, or predict these systems is not keeping pace. Whether you label it AGI today or in three years matters less than the fact that we're heading toward superintelligence, and we don't have a working safety mechanism for it. That's the part I think people should focus on.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes AGI from superintelligence but does not say people have begun using “AGI” to mean superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes current systems as broadly capable and superhuman in some domains, but does not claim they qualify as AGI by outperforming an average human across common tasks on average.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think it's useful to separate three things, because people tend to blur them together.

Current systems, what we have today, I would call narrow AI that's getting less narrow. They're superhuman in some domains already. They beat us at chess, at Go, at protein folding, at certain kinds of pattern recognition. But they're not general. They can't take what they learned in one domain and fluidly apply it to a completely new one the way a human child does.

AGI, artificial general intelligence, is the point where a system can do any cognitive task a human can do, at roughly human level. And I want to be careful here, because the moment you get general human-level intelligence in a machine, you don't stay there. A machine doesn't have the biological constraints we have. It runs faster, it doesn't sleep, it can be copied, it can read every paper ever written in a weekend. So AGI, in my view, is not a stable destination. It's a very short stop on the way to superintelligence.

Superintelligence is a system that is better than the best humans at essentially everything. Science, engineering, social manipulation, strategy. And that's the part people underestimate. Once you have an agent that is smarter than you in every relevant dimension, you can no longer predict what it will do, and you can no longer reliably control it. That's not a technical detail, that's the whole problem. You can't test it, because any test you design, it understands better than you do. You can't verify it, because the verification itself requires a level of intelligence you don't have.

So when people ask me, how far are we, I think the honest answer is that we don't know, and that's exactly what worries me. The gap between what we have now and AGI could be much smaller than it looks, and the gap between AGI and superintelligence could be measured in months, not decades. And my concern is that we are racing toward something we have no idea how to make safe, and we're treating that as an engineering problem we'll solve later. I don't think we get a "later."

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate generality from level of capability. Generality is about the range of problems a system can handle. Intelligence is about how well it handles them. So an artificial general intelligence would be able to learn and perform across a broad range of domains, roughly at a human level. Superintelligence would exceed human capabilities across those domains, including science, engineering, and perhaps understanding human behavior.

Current systems make those distinctions a little messy. They can be superhuman at particular tasks and still fail at things a child finds obvious. Being extraordinarily good at chess doesn't make you generally intelligent. But a system that can write code, discuss philosophy, analyze images, and solve unfamiliar problems is clearly more general than a chess program.

The question is whether that breadth comes with reliable reasoning, learning, and the ability to accomplish things independently. We shouldn't confuse an impressive answer with a robust capability. And we shouldn't assume that reaching human-level general intelligence would be a stable stopping point. Human intelligence isn't some theoretical ceiling. It's just the level evolution happened to produce in us.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of AGI as a system that can perform across the range of cognitive tasks humans can perform, rather than being specialized in one narrow domain. Superintelligence goes beyond that: it exceeds the best human capabilities across essentially all those domains, including scientific research, engineering, and strategic planning.

Current systems make the distinction interesting because their capabilities are uneven. They can outperform most humans on certain tasks and then fail at something a child would find straightforward. So being superhuman at chess, or even at many language tasks, doesn’t by itself make a system generally intelligent.

The important question is how broadly it can learn, adapt, and reliably solve unfamiliar problems. And if we reach human-level general intelligence, I wouldn’t assume it stays at that level for long. Human intelligence is a reference point, not necessarily a ceiling.
